common_name: Orville Fay Siberian Iris (First Tetraploid Blue Self with Dark Veining)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in spring or early fall in moist, fertile, humus-rich soil in full sun to light shade.

directions: Set divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Currier McEwen and notable as one of the first tetraploid Siberian iris cultivars, Orville Fay carries a saturated blue self with darker blue veining on sturdy stems that hold up well through midseason bloom. The tetraploid breeding behind this cultivar gave it heavier substance and larger flowers than older diploid Siberian iris selections, a trait later breeders built on extensively. Clumps tolerate wetter soil than bearded iris and need dividing only every several years, ideally in early fall or right after bloom.

common_name: Harpswell Happiness Siberian Iris (Ruffled Creamy White with Yellow-Green Throat)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade in spring or early fall.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by noted Siberian iris hybridizer Currier McEwen, Harpswell Happiness bears ruffled creamy white standards and falls washed with yellow-green at the base and veined through a buttery signal, giving the flower a soft, glowing quality distinct from pure white selections. It is valued for blooming over an extended stretch rather than the brief flush typical of many Siberian iris, keeping the clump in flower for a longer window each season. Like other Siberian iris it shrugs off wetter soil better than bearded types and can go years between divisions.

common_name: Pansy Purple Siberian Iris (Rich True-Purple Self)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by Currier McEwen, Pansy Purple is named for its rich, true pansy-purple color, a deep saturated self-color that reads darker and more intense than many blue-purple Siberian iris selections. The simple, unpatterned flowers show off the color at its purest against narrow, grass-like clumps of foliage. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs dividing only occasionally, best done in early fall or right after bloom.

common_name: Sea Shadows Siberian Iris (Two-Tone Blue with Turquoise Style Arms)

planting.note: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Plant divisions a couple of inches deep in moist, fertile soil in full sun to light partial shade. Bred by British hybridizer Merton Brummitt from a White Swirl x Tycoon cross, Sea Shadows opens medium blue at the base of its falls and standards, fading to a lighter blue toward the ruffled edges with darker veining and turquoise style arms, a subtle color-shadowing effect that gives the cultivar its name. Floriferous stems make it a reliable cut flower in addition to a garden plant, and it has gone on to parent several other Siberian iris introductions. It tolerates wetter soil than bearded iris and needs dividing only every several years.

common_name: Eleanor Parry Japanese Iris (Historic Double-Flowered Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, since Japanese iris want far more water through the growing season than Siberian or bearded types. Registered by hybridizer John Childs in the 1920s, Eleanor Parry is one of the older named Japanese iris cultivars still in circulation, carrying the fully double, flattened flower form prized in the group. Site it at a pond edge or low spot where the soil stays damp through summer, since it resents drying out during active growth but equally dislikes standing water over winter. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Gracieuse Japanese Iris (White with Violet-Blue Brushed Edges)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, keeping the root zone damp through the growing season. An early twentieth-century French-raised Japanese iris, Gracieuse carries large white flowers brushed with violet-blue along the edges and veining, centered on a small yellow signal that pulls the eye into each bloom. The slender, upright foliage stays attractive as a vertical accent well after bloom finishes, making it a useful structural plant at a pond margin. Divide crowded clumps in early spring every few years, since Japanese iris bloom best when not left to overcrowd themselves.

common_name: Moonlight Waves Japanese Iris (Historic White with Lime-Green Center)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade.

directions: Plant divisions in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun to light partial shade, since Japanese iris need steady moisture through summer to perform well. Dating to around 1910 and among the older named Japanese iris still offered today, Moonlight Waves opens large, flat white flowers with a lime-green center that diffuses softly into the petal base, giving the bloom a luminous quality at dusk. Strap-like mid-green foliage forms an upright clump that holds its shape through the season, useful as a textural anchor at a pond edge or bog garden. Divide crowded clumps in early spring every few years to keep bloom vigorous.
